$comment: The Merlin Agent Linux collection manifest.
THIS FILE IS THE COMPLETE LIST OF WHAT THE AGENT READS THROUGH osquery ON LINUX. Every query
below runs through osqueryi and nothing else is queried. An administrator can paste any of
them into osqueryi on their own machine and get byte-identical output.
LINUX ALSO READS FOUR THINGS FROM THE FILESYSTEM, because osquery has no table for them:
/sys/firmware/efi/efivars/SecureBoot-*   — whether Secure Boot is enforced
/sys/class/tpm/tpm0/tpm_version_major    — whether a TPM is present, and its version
/etc/login.defs, /etc/security/pwquality.conf — the local password policy
the package database's modification time — when software was last installed
plus the host firewall's own status command (ufw, firewall-cmd, or nft). Those five are
listed in docs/collection-manifest.md and are read with no shell interpolation of any kind.
NOTHING HERE READS WHO IS SIGNED IN. There is no query for the logged-in user, the session,
the tty or any mail address. The two account queries return LOCAL ACCOUNT names, which are
machine configuration — see their own comments.
A query that fails or returns nothing produces a NULL reading, never a false one. Merlin
treats null as 'not observed' and will not raise a nonconformity from it.
QUERIES RUN IN THE ORDER LISTED HERE, AND THE ORDER IS DELIBERATE. A collection is bounded so
it cannot hold the machine lock past the point where the updater gives up waiting for it, and
on a machine where osquery answers slowly that bound is reached before the end of this list.
Whatever is left is reported as NOT OBSERVED, so the security-posture queries come first and
the inventory ones last: losing a hostname degrades a device page, while losing disk encryption
or the firewall loses the reading the ISMS exists to take.
A PRIVACY-CRITICAL QUERY. The disk_encryption table also carries `uid` and `user_uuid` —
'currently authenticated user if available' — which identify the person who unlocked the
volume. This query names exactly the columns it wants, so those are never returned to the
agent at all: the restriction is enforced by the query rather than by the agent
remembering to ignore them.
Reported to Merlin as ONE machine-level reading, not per volume. A fully encrypted Linux
install still has an unencrypted /boot — that is how the scheme works — so passing the
raw rows into Merlin's weakest-volume-wins reduction would report every correctly
encrypted machine as unencrypted. See LinuxNormaliser for the trade this makes.
disk_encryption.sql: SELECT name, encrypted, type FROM disk_encryption;
disk_encryption.purpose: Whether any block device is protected by LUKS (A.8.24).

$comment: Returns LOCAL ACCOUNT names, not the identity of whoever is signed in. Linux has no
single administrators group, so all three conventional names are matched — a machine
using `wheel` and one using `sudo` must not read differently.
local_admins.sql: SELECT u.username FROM users u JOIN user_groups ug ON u.uid = ug.uid JOIN groups g ON ug.gid = g.gid WHERE g.groupname IN ('sudo', 'wheel', 'admin');
local_admins.purpose: Local accounts holding administrative rights through group membership (A.8.2).

$comment: Collected SEPARATELY from the group query and unioned with it. An account with uid 0 has
root's rights without being in any administrators group, and it is the more serious of
the two findings — reading only the group query would let it go uncounted.
root_accounts.sql: SELECT username FROM users WHERE uid = 0;

$comment: `platform` is the stable distribution id — ubuntu, debian, rhel, fedora — and is what
Merlin's end-of-life table keys on. `name` is the marketing name, which a release can
restyle; both travel so the display value and the lookup value cannot drift.
os_version.sql: SELECT name, version, build, platform, platform_like FROM os_version;
os_version.purpose: Distribution, version and id — what end-of-support is judged against.

system_volume.sql: SELECT blocks, blocks_available, blocks_size FROM mounts WHERE path = '/';
system_volume.purpose: Free space on the root filesystem (A.8.6 capacity).

system_info.sql: SELECT hostname, uuid, hardware_serial, hardware_vendor, hardware_model, cpu_brand FROM system_info;
system_info.purpose: Machine identity, and the serial used to reconcile against the asset register.

kernel.purpose: Running kernel release, reported as the build so a machine pending a reboot after a kernel update is visible.
